316.title: What is man? (Psalm 8)
316.hook: looking at the heavens, the psalmist marvels that God made us "but little lower than the angels"
316.howItsDone: Psalm 8 is read as part of personal and communal psalm recitation, and its question, what is man, is quoted often in Jewish teaching on human dignity and responsibility.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one: a tree planted by streams of water. Your line was planted by the streams. Did you water your roots? Day three hundred sixteen.

segments.voice: Have you ever been somewhere truly dark at night? Away from the city, no streetlights, and you look up, and the sky is crowded. Thousands of stars. The smear of the Milky Way. And two feelings arrive at once. First: I am so small. And then, strangely, the second: and yet I'm here, seeing this. Three thousand years ago, someone stood under the same sky, felt both of those at once, and wrote them down as a song. Today: Psalm eight.
screen: `A SKY CROWDED WITH STARS.` → `I AM SO SMALL.` → `AND YET I'M HERE, SEEING IT.`

segments.voice: Psalm eight is a night-sky psalm. The psalmist looks up at the heavens, the work of God's fingers, the moon and the stars set in their places. Fingers: as if the whole sky were delicate handiwork. And then the question: "What is man, that Thou art mindful of him?" In Hebrew, mah enosh. Enosh is a word for a human being that leans toward frailty, a creature that gets sick and gets old. Next to the stars, what are we? Why would God even notice? But the psalm doesn't stop at small. It answers its own question with something startling: Thou hast made him "but little lower than the angels," and crowned him with glory and honor. Small and crowned. Both at once. The psalm then gives people a job: to care for the works of God's hands, the sheep and oxen, the birds and the fish. Not to own the world, but to be trusted with it. There's a lovely puzzle in the Hebrew, too. The word translated angels is elohim, which usually means God. The old Aramaic translation and many Jewish commentators read it as angels, divine beings, and the 1917 Jewish translation follows them. Others read it: a little lower than God. Either way, the point is the same. Under an enormous sky, a fragile human being is given a crown. The psalm begins and ends with the same line, praising how majestic God's name is in all the earth. The human being sits right in the middle.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the night sky. If it's night where you are, step outside or to a window and look up. If it's daytime, look at the sky anyway, or close your eyes and picture the stars. Settle, and breathe. Let yourself feel small. Really small. Then let the second feeling come: that you, of all things, are the one looking. Hold both. Small, and crowned. If you pray, you can say the psalm's question to God: what is man, that Thou art mindful of him? The bell holds the time.
What is man? Psalm eight's question under the stars, and its answer: fragile, and yet made but little lower than the angels.

317.title: The Lord is my shepherd (Psalm 23)
317.hook: sung at the third Shabbat meal and read at funerals
317.howItsDone: Many Jewish communities sing Psalm 23 at the third Shabbat meal, and some on Friday night too; it is also read at funerals, at the unveiling of a gravestone and when visiting the sick.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm eight under the stars. Your line was a little lower than angels. Did you feel small, and crowned? Today, the most famous psalm of all. Day three hundred seventeen.

segments.voice: It's late on a Saturday afternoon. The light is going gold. Shabbat is almost over, and around a table, people eat a last small meal, and someone starts to sing, slowly: Mizmor le-David. A psalm of David. The Lord is my shepherd. Now picture a very different scene: a cemetery, a family at a graveside, and someone reading the same words. The same psalm at the gentlest hour of the week, and at the hardest hour of a life. Today: Psalm twenty-three.
screen: `SHABBAT'S LAST GOLDEN HOUR.` → `A GRAVESIDE.` → `THE SAME PSALM AT BOTH.`

segments.voice: It starts: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." In Hebrew, lo echsar: I will not lack. Not I'll have everything. I won't be missing what I need. David was a shepherd before he was a king, and the picture is precise. A shepherd in the hills of Judea had to find grass in dry country and water that was calm enough for sheep to drink. So: green pastures, still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me on straight paths. Then comes the valley. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, "I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." Listen closely to what just happened. Up to now, the psalm has been talking about God: He leads me, He restores me. In the dark valley, it switches. Now it talks to God: You are with me. When things are good, God is described. When things are dark, God is addressed. That's exactly why this psalm is read at gravesides. And why it's sung as Shabbat fades, a quiet reassurance before a new week begins. Then the scene changes again: a table set in front of me, a cup that overflows, and a home in the house of the Lord for long days. The psalm doesn't pretend there is no valley. It walks straight through it, with company.

318.title: Clean hands (Psalm 24)
318.hook: who may climb the mountain? "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart"
318.howItsDone: Many congregations sing Psalm 24 as the Torah is returned to the ark on weekdays, and observant Jews wash their hands ritually, with a blessing, on waking and before eating bread.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord is my shepherd, the psalm that walks through the valley. Your line was I shall not want. Did you name one thing you're not lacking? Day three hundred eighteen.
screen: `I SHALL NOT WANT.`

segments.voice: Think about the places you can't just walk into. A hospital operating room: you scrub first. A friend's home: you knock. A job interview: you prepare for days. We understand, without anyone telling us, that some places ask something of us before we enter. Now imagine a crowd of pilgrims at the foot of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, looking up the hill. Someone calls out a question, and the whole crowd answers. Psalm twenty-four may be exactly that: a question at the gate.
screen: `SCRUB BEFORE THE OPERATING ROOM.` → `KNOCK BEFORE YOU ENTER.` → `A QUESTION AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens by saying the whole earth belongs to God, and everyone in it. Then the question: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the LORD?" Who shall stand in His holy place? And the answer: "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart". In Hebrew: neki khapayim u-var levav. Clean hands, a pure heart. Notice what isn't on the list. Not who's the richest, the most learned, from the right family. The entrance requirements are hands and heart. Hands are what you do: how you treat people, what you take, what you give, whether your business is honest. The psalm spells it out: someone who hasn't sworn deceitfully. The heart is what's going on inside: your intentions, whether you mean it. Both matter. Clean hands with a hidden agenda aren't enough. A good heart that never acts isn't enough either. Then the psalm bursts into a kind of drama: lift up your heads, O ye gates, that the King of glory may come in. Who is the King of glory? Many scholars think this was sung antiphonally, one group calling, another answering, maybe as the ark came up to Jerusalem. Today, in many synagogues, this psalm is sung as the Torah scroll is carried back to the ark on weekdays: the gates lift, and the Torah goes home. And Jewish life has a daily echo of clean hands: the ritual washing on waking and before eating bread, with a blessing. Not because the hands are dirty. Because the next thing they do matters.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash your hands with intention. If you can, go to a sink now. If not, do this the next time you wash. Let the water run over your hands slowly. Feel it. As you wash, think of one thing your hands will do today: write, cook, hold someone, fix something, type a message. Ask that it be clean: honest, kind. Then dry them, and notice your heart. What do you mean by the day ahead? If you pray, you can say so to God. The bell holds the time.
Clean hands. Psalm twenty-four's answer to who may climb the mountain of the Lord: clean hands, and a pure heart. What you do, and what you mean.

319.title: Ashrei (Psalm 145)
319.hook: said three times a day; the Talmud praises whoever says it daily (Berakhot 4b)
319.howItsDone: Ashrei is said twice in the morning service and once at the start of the afternoon service; many people say the open-hand verse with special concentration, and some touch their tefillin as they say it.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm twenty-four: who may climb the mountain? Your line was clean hands, pure heart. Did you check what your hands would do next? Day three hundred nineteen.

segments.voice: If you've ever been to a weekday service in a synagogue, you've heard it, maybe without knowing its name. A fast, murmured rush of Hebrew, everyone at their own speed, one of the most-said passages in all of Jewish prayer. It's said twice every morning and once every afternoon. Three times a day, every day, for a lifetime. Adds up to tens of thousands of times. It begins with the word Ashrei, and it has a small mystery hidden in its alphabet. Today: Ashrei.
screen: `A FAST, MURMURED RUSH OF HEBREW.` → `THREE TIMES A DAY.` → `A MYSTERY IN THE ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: Ashrei means happy, or fortunate: happy are those who dwell in Your house. Two opening verses from other psalms lead in, and then comes the heart of it, Psalm one hundred forty-five. It's an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, aleph, bet, gimmel, all the way through. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says that whoever recites it three times a day is assured a place in the world to come. Then it asks why this psalm, of all psalms. Because it goes through the alphabet? Other psalms do that too. The answer: because it goes through the alphabet and it contains this verse: "Thou openest Thy hand, and satisfiest every living thing with favour." Every living thing. Not just people, not just the righteous. The whole world, fed from an open hand. Many people slow down at that verse and say it with special attention. Now the mystery. One letter is missing. There's no verse for nun. The Talmud notices, and gives an answer. Nun would bring to mind a verse from the prophet Amos about Israel fallen, so the psalm leaves it out. And then, with the very next letter, samekh, it says: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall." The fall isn't mentioned. The catch comes first. So Ashrei holds an alphabet with a gap in it, and a hand stretched out over the gap. Said three times a day, it keeps coming back to the same picture: an open hand, and someone holding up whoever falls.
screen: `ASHREI: HAPPY ARE THEY.` · `AN ALPHABET PSALM.` · `THOU OPENEST THY HAND.` · `NO NUN: THE CATCH BEFORE THE FALL.` · then, large: `THOU OPENEST THY HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm one forty-five once. If you have it nearby, read it slowly, all the way through, and slow down at the open-hand verse. If not, try this. Settle, and breathe. Rest your hands in your lap, palms up. Open. Think of what has come to you through open hands today: food, a kind word, a roof, a breath. Let each one land. Then think of someone who's fallen lately, and imagine holding them up. If you pray, you can say the open-hand verse. The bell holds the time.
Ashrei. Happy are they. Psalm one forty-five, said three times a day: an alphabet with one letter missing, and an open hand that feeds every living thing.

320.title: A psalm for each day
320.hook: each weekday has its own psalm, once sung by the Levites in the Temple
320.howItsDone: Near the end of the morning service, the Song of the Day is introduced with 'today is the first (second, third…) day of the week, on which the Levites used to say in the Temple' and then the day's psalm is recited.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashrei, the alphabet with a gap and an open hand. Your line was thou openest thy hand. Did you pause and open your palms? Day three hundred twenty.
screen: `THOU OPENEST THY HAND.`

segments.voice: Some people have a song for Monday mornings. Some families have Friday pizza, or Sunday pancakes. We like it when days have their own flavor, so the week isn't one long gray blur. Jewish prayer did this a very long time ago, with music. Every day of the week has its own psalm. And near the end of the morning service, someone announces, almost like a radio host: today is the second day of the week. And then comes the song. Today: a psalm for each day.
screen: `SUNDAY PANCAKES, FRIDAY PIZZA.` → `EVERY DAY ITS OWN FLAVOR.` → `EVERY DAY ITS OWN PSALM.`

segments.voice: The custom comes from the Temple in Jerusalem. The Mishnah, in tractate Tamid, lists the psalm the Levites sang each day as the daily offering was made. Sunday, Psalm twenty-four. Monday, forty-eight. Tuesday, eighty-two. Wednesday, ninety-four. Thursday, eighty-one. Friday, ninety-three. And on Shabbat, ninety-two, the psalm that calls itself a song for the Sabbath day. The Temple is long gone, but the songs are still sung. In the prayer book, each one begins with a line like: today is the first day of the week, on which the Levites used to say in the Temple. Notice something. Jewish weekdays don't have names. They have numbers, counting toward Shabbat. First day, second day, third. Every weekday is a step on the way to the seventh. The Talmud explains why each psalm fits its day, by linking it to the days of creation. On the first day, God made the world and owned it, so Sunday's psalm opens: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." On the sixth day, creation was finished and God reigned over it, so Friday's psalm opens: the Lord reigns, clothed in majesty. Each day of the week remembers its day of the first week. So when you wake up on an ordinary Tuesday, the tradition says it isn't ordinary. It has its own place in the story of creation, and its own song.

Friday, ninety-three. Shabbat, ninety-two. If you can look it up, read the first few lines. If not, settle, and breathe, and think about which day of creation today remembers. Light? Sky? Land and plants? Sun and moon? Fish and birds? Animals and people? Rest? Notice it around you today. If you pray, you can say today's psalm. The bell holds the time.
A psalm for each day. The songs the Levites sang in the Temple, one for every day of the week, still said at the end of the morning service.

321.title: Hallel (Psalms 113–118)
321.hook: psalms of praise sung on festivals and new moons
321.howItsDone: Hallel is recited after the morning Amidah on Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot, Hanukkah and Rosh Chodesh, in full or in a shortened form, and it is also sung at the Passover seder.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a psalm for each day of the week. Your line was each day has a song. Did you notice what made today different? Today, the songs for the special days. Day three hundred twenty-one.
screen: `EACH DAY HAS A SONG.`

segments.voice: You know the word even if you've never been in a synagogue. Hallelujah. It's in hymns, in gospel songs, in a famous chorus by Handel, in pop songs. People shout it when the team wins. It's Hebrew, and it means praise God. Hallelu, praise, and Yah, a short name of God. Now take that first half, hallel, and make it a noun. In Jewish prayer, Hallel is the name of a set of six psalms, the ones pulled out for the happiest days of the year. Today: Hallel.
screen: `HALLELUJAH, IN EVERY LANGUAGE.` → `HALLELU-YAH: PRAISE GOD.` → `SIX PSALMS FOR HAPPY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Hallel is Psalms one hundred thirteen to one hundred eighteen, said together as one long song. It's sung on the three pilgrimage festivals, Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, on all eight days of Hanukkah, and on Rosh Chodesh, the new moon. Often the congregation stands, and many communities sing it out loud to lively tunes. The psalms move through a whole story. Praise from the rising of the sun to its setting. Then Psalm one hundred fourteen: when Israel came out of Egypt, the sea looked and fled, the mountains skipped like rams. Then thanks for being rescued. And at the end, the great refrain of Psalm one hundred eighteen: give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy endures forever. And this line: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." On some days, like the new moon and the last days of Passover, a shorter version is said, with parts left out. The Talmud gives a reason for the Passover custom: the Egyptians drowned in the sea, and one does not sing full praise over the fall of any of God's creatures. There's another telling gap. Hallel is not said on Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur. The Talmud imagines the angels asking why, and the answer is: the King sits in judgment, the books of life and death are open, and should Israel sing? Hallel knows when to sing loudly, when to sing less, and when to be quiet.

Let one reason to be glad about this particular day come up. If you pray, you can make it your praise. The bell holds the time.

322.title: A song for the Sabbath (Psalm 92)
322.hook: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree"

segments.voice: Friday evening. The candles are lit. In the synagogue, people have been singing psalms to welcome Shabbat, one after another. Then comes a particular one, and for many, that's the moment the week is truly over. The work is done, the phone is off, Shabbat has arrived. The psalm announces itself in its first line: a song for the Sabbath day. And then, strangely, it never mentions the Sabbath again. Today: Psalm ninety-two, and the palm tree inside it.
screen: `FRIDAY EVENING, CANDLES LIT.` → `THE MOMENT SHABBAT ARRIVES.` → `A SABBATH SONG THAT NEVER SAYS SABBATH.`

segments.voice: It begins: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." In Hebrew, mizmor shir le-yom ha-Shabbat. It's the Levites' song for Shabbat from the Temple, and it's said on Friday night and again on Shabbat morning. Then it gets going: it's good to give thanks to the Lord, to tell of His kindness in the morning and His faithfulness in the night. And then, not a word about rest, candles or the seventh day. Why is this the Sabbath psalm? The rabbis gave answers. The Mishnah ends its list of daily psalms by calling this one a song for the time to come, a day that will be entirely Sabbath and rest. A midrash says Adam himself sang it, on the first Shabbat of the world. And many readers say: it's about what Shabbat lets you see. During the week, you're too busy to notice that the proud and the cruel spring up like grass and wither. On Shabbat, you stop long enough to see what lasts. And then the famous line: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon." Two trees. The palm, which gives sweet fruit. The cedar, which grows tall and strong and lasts for centuries. Some commentators say you need both: sweetness and strength. And the psalm adds that these trees still bear fruit in old age, full of sap and green. It closes a week of psalms: what is man, the shepherd, clean hands, Ashrei, a psalm for each day, Hallel, and today, the Sabbath song.
screen: `MIZMOR SHIR LE-YOM HA-SHABBAT.` · `NO WORD ABOUT THE SABBATH?` · `THE PALM AND THE CEDAR.` · `FRUIT IN OLD AGE.` · then, large: `FLOURISH LIKE A PALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or hum, the Shabbat way. Whatever day it is, you can taste it. Settle, and breathe. Put down your work, even in your mind, for two minutes. Hum a gentle tune, any tune, or the niggun from a few weeks ago. As you hum, picture a palm tree: tall, sweet fruit, swaying. Then a cedar: deep roots, strong. Ask yourself: where am I sweet? Where am I strong? If it's Shabbat where you are, let this be part of it. If you pray, you can give thanks. The bell holds the time.
A song for the Sabbath. Psalm ninety-two, sung as Shabbat arrives: the righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like the cedar, bearing fruit even in old age.
screen: `A SONG FOR THE SABBATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: flourish like a palm. Today, be sweet and be strong, once each: one kind word, and one thing you stand firm on. Day three hundred twenty-two.
